title: The story beyond the telemetry
description: Focused chapters on electric racing, technology, service, Japan and Zen, and the video archives that connect them.

pages.title: Electric first. Fast followed.
pages.lede: I came to motorcycles through electricity first. A commuter Zero became a Bonneville record bike, then a development platform for racing, charging, and software—and took me to Pikes Peak.

sections.title: A commuter motorcycle became a record bike.
body: The measured one-mile record was 101.652 mph on a modified production Zero S ZF6 under 150 kg, certified through AMA and FIM timing. The work connected riding, software, development testing, and the early DigiNow and Hollywood Electrics community.
The point was never speed alone. It was learning what electric drivetrains could become when riders, engineers, and builders treated the machine as a platform.

sections.title: Development work moved from the salt to the mountain.
body: Official Pikes Peak results record the #111 Zero S in 2013 and a third-place Electric Production finish on a Zero SR in 2015. Each run joined motorcycle setup, energy strategy, charging, software, and the realities of a changing mountain course.

sections.title: Long distance exposed the infrastructure problem.
body: An 821-mile, 23-hour reconnaissance ride helped prepare for a 1,000-mile electric Iron Butt attempt. The published record supports the preparation and route test—not a claim of completed certification.

pages.title: From artificial vision to local-first tools.
pages.lede: My favorite technology gives people more agency: restoring a signal, exposing a hidden system, shortening the distance between an idea and a useful tool.

sections.title: Technology in service of sight.
body: At Second Sight Medical Products, I worked with a development team on artificial-vision technology intended to help blind people see. The work belongs to a large clinical, engineering, research, and patient community; this page does not reduce that shared effort to a single inventor story.

sections.title: Charging hardware became a company, a race program, and a public archive.
body: DigiNow grew from practical electric-motorcycle charging problems into adapters, Super Charger systems, vehicle experiments, racing footage, and prototypes that connected phones and tablets to motorcycles.

sections.title: Browser-owned data, made understandable.
body: DBOPFS Studio is a local-first Chromium workspace for exploring, editing, previewing, printing, and managing application data stored in origin-private OPFS. It makes a normally invisible browser data layer inspectable without turning it into a cloud service.

sections.title: ActionScript 3 was my first ECMAScript language.
body: I loved Flash before the browser platform moved on. ActionScript 3 taught me the shape of ECMAScript, and that lineage still informs how I write traditional JavaScript: direct, portable, understandable, and close to the platform.

pages.title: Build for people. Stay useful.
pages.lede: Military service, community leadership, overseas intelligence and technology work, and mental-health advocacy all shaped the same operating principle: make the work practical, humane, and accountable.

sections.title: Service changed how I understand systems and responsibility.
body: I served in the United States Air Force and later worked with military-adjacent organizations, international teams, and intelligence and technology contractors around the world. The public version of that history stays deliberately high level: the lasting lesson is that technical choices always land on real people.

sections.title: Support should feel human before it feels institutional.
body: My advocacy centers practical tools, community, and honest conversations that respect lived experience—especially for veterans navigating transition, isolation, and mental-health challenges. I care about technology that lowers friction without pretending software can replace human care.

sections.title: Leadership is something people practice together.
body: I have worked closely with Rotary and Rotary Youth Leadership Awards communities. Their emphasis on service, ethical leadership, and developing young people fits the same pattern I value in open source: share responsibility, make room for others, and leave a system stronger.

pages.title: Japan, Zen, and the discipline of attention.
pages.lede: Living and attending high school in Japan gave me a vocabulary of practice long before I had a vocabulary for product design, leadership, or engineering.

facts.label: Judo · Kyudo · Shodo · Kado · Sado · Budo

sections.title: The arts were different. The demand for attention was the same.
body: While living and attending high school in Japan, I studied judo, kyudo, shodo, kado, sado, and budo. I do not present that list as mastery. It marks an early encounter with forms that make repetition, posture, care, and presence visible.

sections.title: Zen study continued after I returned to the United States.
body: My Zen practice began in the Rinzai-ji tradition after I returned from overseas work. Bodhi Manda Zen Center provides public context for that lineage and its history; this page describes my personal chronology rather than claiming a formal title or credential.

sections.title: Clarity over noise is not a slogan. It is a constraint.
body: Attention shapes how I build: prefer the direct path, make hidden state visible, avoid ceremony that does not serve the user, and keep moving without confusing motion for progress. Entrepreneurship becomes a practice of creating useful things, learning in public, and serving people well.

pages.title: Different channels. One connected life.
pages.lede: Music, electric racing, charging hardware, AI experiments, open-source work, and product demos each have their own archive.

sections.title: AI Wizard
body: The music channel holds releases made through human experience and AI-assisted craft. It is the listening counterpart to the full catalog on this site.

sections.title: NewZeroland / Brandon Nozaki Miller
body: The channel began around electric motorcycles and grew to include charging, inventing, racing, travel, and the practical life around early electric mobility.

sections.title: DigiNow Inc
body: The DigiNow archive connects charging hardware, race weekends, prototype interfaces, and the experiments that sometimes became projects or companies.

sections.title: AI Nerd
body: The AI Nerd archive covers on-device models, early mental-health and veteran-support prototypes, open-source projects, and practical guidance on development, architecture, engineering, and testing.
